sentences.text: The present appeal has been filed inter alia on grounds that the ld. executing court failed to record and consider the detailed submissions advanced by the JD/appellant regarding the maintainability and limitation aspects of execution petitions wherein the order assailed was passed.

It is further adumbrated that the trial court erred in placing undue reliance upon Apex Court judgment in the case titled as Periyammal (Dead) through LRs. & Ors. vs V. Rajamani & Anr. Etc., Civil Appeal Nos.3640- 3642 of 2025; directing that the execution petitions should be disposed of within six months, which was merely a directive for expeditious disposal and not a binding precedent overriding statutory law.

sentences.text: It is contended by appellant that the executing court failed to appreciate that the said direction cannot override or dilute the limitation period or statutory preconditions prescribed for execution of a decree/order u/s 125(3) Cr.P.C.

The ld. counsel for the appellant canvassed that the execution of a decree/order of maintenance is subject to limitation and can only be initiated within a reasonable period (in this case, one year from default) and the impugned order Rahul Bhati vs Karishma Bhati on 17 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/7840842/

It is prayed by ld. counsel for the appellant that the impugned order be set aside as the same is bad in law.

sentences.text: Upon service, the respondent/wife appeared and filed a reply wherein she stated that the impugned order dated 15.10.2025 was legal, proper, well reasoned and passed in accordance with settled principles of law and therefore, does not warrant any interference u/s 29 of the DV Act.

Ld. 
counsel for respondent pointed out that it is the appellant who had failed to comply with the valid and subsisting order dated 06.12.2018 (awarding maintenance) and he is now attempting to delay the rightful execution of maintenance order.
He submitted that the respondent was compelled to file execution petitions only on account of the willful and continuous non-compliance of order by the appellant.
He further canvassed that respondent/wife has been suffering for years without financial support and arrears of maintenance payable by appellant exceed Rs.13 lakhs (Rs.16,500 x 83 months approx.).

He also submitted that the present appeal is nothing but a desperate attempt to delay payment and harass the respondent who has been deprived of her lawful maintenance for over 7 years despite a court order that had attained finality.
He prayed that the appeal be dismissed and heavy cost be imposed upon the appellant.

sentences.text: In our view, the DV Act is a piece of civil code which is applicable to every woman in India irrespective of her religious affiliation and/or social background for a more effective protection of her rights guaranteed under the Constitution and in order to protect women victims of domestic violence occurring in a domestic relationship.

Therefore, the expression "joint family"
cannot mean as understood in Hindu Law.
Thus, the expression "family members living together as a joint family", means the members living jointly as a family.

In such an interpretation, even a girl child/children who is/are cared for as foster children also have a right to live in a shared household and are conferred with the right under sub-section (1) of Section 17 of the DV Act.
When such a girl child or woman becomes an aggrieved person, the protection of sub-section (2) of Section 17 comes into play."
(emphasis added)

13. In fact, the very purpose of enacting the DV Act was to provide for a remedy which is an amalgamation of civil rights of the complainant i.e aggrieved person.
Intention was to protect women against violence of any kind, especially that occurring within the family as the civil law does not address this phenomenon in its entirety.
It is treated as an offence under Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code.

The purpose of enacting the law was to provide a remedy in the civil law for the protection of women from being victims of domestic violence and to prevent the occurrence of domestic violence in the society.........

The DV Act is a beneficial legislation enacted to prevent vagrancy, penury and destitution, therefore the same ought to be interpreted in a manner which aids in achieving its noble objectives rather than thwarting justice.

sentences.text: For enforcement/execution of orders of maintenance, it is directed that an order or decree of maintenance may be enforced Under Section 28A of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955; Section 20(6) of the D.V. Act; and Section 128 of Cr.PC, as may be applicable.
The order of maintenance may be enforced as a money decree of a civil court as per the provisions of the CPC, more particularly Sections 51, 55, 58, 60 read with Order 21.
Since, the order of maintenance has to be treated as a money decree of a civil court, therefore, the provisions of law for enforcement of money decree shall come into play.
The money decree as per Schedule appended to the Limitation Act, 1963 can be got executed within a period of 12 years from the date when the decree becomes enforceable, as prescribed in Article 136.

Therefore, the arguments that recovery of maintenance awarded under the DV Act is governed by Section 125(3)
Cr.PC falls flat.

There is no illegality or impropriety in the order dated 15.10.2025 passed by the Ld.
Executing Court.
The execution petitions were filed within the prescribed period of limitation and are also maintainable.
The order assailed is in consonance with the extant applicable law.
Accordingly, the present appeal is dismissed being bereft of merit.
Interim order, if any, stands vacated.
Two original DDs in the name of the respondent of Rs.50,000/- each available on record can be collected by the Crl.
